# Display, canvas and runner gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- M5GFX reads a plain `uint32_t` colour as RGB888. `TFT_RED` and friends are
  RGB565 constants. The canvas holds pixels already byte-swapped into the
  display's order (`rgb565()` returns them that way), and the display runs
  with `setSwapBytes(false)`. A swap done by M5GFX on each push cost 10 ms of
  every frame (#23: pushes of 41-45 ms became 31 ms). `px_swap()` turns a
  canvas pixel into ordinary RGB565 and back: only code that reads colour bits
  needs it (the logo loader, `dump_main.c`, tests). A hue-sweeping palette
  stays a rainbow with its bytes swapped (red, green and blue rotate), so only
  pure black and white, or a colour you know (Maze's red flame, its green
  solving path), expose a wrong order on the device. Host frames cannot,
  since the swap happens in the push; compare them with `px_swap` applied.
- A hack that takes colour bits out of pixel values itself (Substrate's alpha
  blend, in `point2rgb`) breaks on swapped pixels without a compile error and
  without a crash. `substrate_single.c` swaps at `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground` so the hack sees ordinary RGB565; its golden-frame test
  fails if either is missing. Searching for `XGetPixel` finds none of this:
  dump every hack before and after a pixel-format change and `cmp` the frames.
  Pyro differs by a few hundred pixels, because it sorts projectiles by pixel
  value and so draws overlaps in another order.
- The display only gets the rows a hack drew. Every canvas write must go
  through `canvas_clear`, `canvas_point`, `hspan` or `canvas_paste_rect`
  (which record a span per row), or call `canvas_mark_dirty`, or the screen
  keeps the old pixels. The overlay text in `main.cpp` is the one deliberate
  bypass: it is written straight into `px`, marked by hand, and restored with
  `canvas_paste_rect`, which marks it again so the next push erases it.
  `test_push_present` replays every hack into a shadow display to catch a
  missed mark. M5GFX keeps a framebuffer for this panel and `endWrite` flushes
  one bounding box around everything written in a `startWrite` batch, so rows
  far apart must not share a batch (two corner pixels cost 11.7 ms together,
  0.1 ms apart). `push_plan` groups rows with a cost model fitted to device
  probes; its calibration shapes must include scattered rows, since compact
  rectangles cannot tell the models apart. Hacks that redraw unchanged pixels
  (CloudLife, Pedal) dirty nearly every row and gain little.
- The panel is round, so only the canvas's disc is pushed (issue #77).
  `canvas_set_disc` (in `main.cpp`) records each row's visible span: centre
  (w/2, h/2), and a pixel counts if any part of it is inside the circle.
  `push_plan` clips every dirty span to it and drops rows left empty. A hack
  with `sync_to_refresh` (Unknown Pleasures) still pushes whole rows, because
  its TE offset was swept for that push (#68). `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` turns off the
  push clip only, for an A/B: GL hacks still clear and fill only the disc
  (`gl.md`). Call `canvas_set_disc` before any `glshim_open`, which keeps a
  pointer to the spans. On the board: CloudLife's full frame 28.0 to 24.8 ms
  (26.2 to 28.4 fps), HexTrail 30.6 to 27.3 ms, Pyro 1.60 to 1.43 ms.
- Do not split a push into more batches than `push_plan`'s greedy grouping
  makes. Each extra flush in one push cost about 0.85 ms on the board, not the
  model's 17 us: a full disc frame in 19 bands took 39.9 ms against 24.7 ms in
  the greedy grouping's three, and per-row `pushImage` calls in one batch cost
  no more than one whole-image call (28.0 against 27.8 ms). The last flush of a
  push seems to finish while the hack draws its next frame; earlier ones are
  waited for. The cost model was fitted to single-flush pushes and cannot see
  this, so a split it rates cheaper can be slower.
- Hacks run on the Arduino `loopTask`, now set to a 16 KB stack in `main.cpp`.
  A hack with big local arrays can still overflow it (Rorschach's 9.6 KB did
  at 8 KB): the device reboots on that hack's first frame, and host tests
  cannot see it. Check the serial log for "Stack canary".
- `M5.update()` samples the buttons only when it runs and keeps no edge, so a
  press during a long hack step vanishes. `main.cpp` runs a 5 ms polling task
  on core 0 into `button_latch`, which needs the pin to hold a level for 30 ms.
  Reading the pin level inside a GPIO interrupt did not work: the release
  bounced and was counted as a second press. Check `press_waited` in the log.
- The runner caps a hack's delay at 10 s, and the loop credits only the push
  (31 ms; it was 41-45 ms between the byte-order fix and #23) against it,
  because a hack's delay is its pause after drawing. Compare device numbers
  with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: Pyro fell from 30 to
  23 fps with no change to Pyro.
- `runner_start` paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before
  `init`, as `screenhack.c` paints the window, or black if it has none.
  Substrate is white; every other hack asks for black or nothing.
- Overlay modes cycle on a tap: nothing, name badge, QR code, fps, battery. The
  badge, the QR code and the info line share the stamp/unstamp path, and
  `kPatchMaxH` (140) must cover the text block plus its outline: the badge
  is two lines, and `stampText` drops any line that would not fit. The
  battery is polled every 30 s (`M5.Power.getBatteryLevel()`; negative means a
  failed read, so the last good level stays). The QR code is encoded once at
  boot with M5GFX's `lgfx_qrcode` (`buildQr`, lowest version that holds
  `QR_URL`) into a 328 px white square, the biggest square inside the round
  screen. Each frame only copies it over the canvas and back (it reuses
  `infoPatch`, so that buffer is sized for the QR), and 328 rows are pushed
  every frame while it shows. The badge stamps 48 outline copies per frame and
  adds about 16 to 20 ms to `push=`. Read `wait=` as well as fps: a hack with
  delay slack (Galaxy) hides it, one running flat out (Squiral) does not.
- `lgfx_qrcode.h` (M5GFX's QR encoder, included at the top of `main.cpp`)
  defines `MODE_*`, `ECC_*` and `LOCK_VERSION`, which clash with other code, so
  `main.cpp` `#undef`s them straight after the include. Its init returns
  nonzero when the text is too long for a version; `buildQr` tries versions 1
  to 40 and, if none fits, leaves `qrPixels` null so the tap cycle skips QR.
- Overlay text (`main.cpp`) is stamped into the canvas, pushed, then the
  pixels under it are restored. Drawing on the display after `pushImage`
  flickered badly, because the next push erases it. The canvas must end each
  frame exactly as the hack left it.
- Tearing. The panel scans its memory 60 times a second and `pushImage` is not
  synchronised with it, so for a refresh the top of the screen shows one
  picture and the rest another. A thin line that moves a few pixels a frame can
  fall in the gap and vanish for a frame (Unknown Pleasures' flicker: a flat
  stretch of one line gone for about 17 ms). The panel's TE line is on GPIO 38
  (`OLED_TE`), M5GFX programs it (`0x35`, `0x44` at line 466) and nothing waits
  for it. It pulses every 16.82 ms for 1.1 ms. A full push is 20.6 ms copying
  into M5GFX's framebuffer plus 11.7 ms flushing to the panel (split by an
  outer `startWrite()` around the `pushImage`; the flush happens at the
  `endWrite`). `HackEntry::sync_to_refresh` (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`) starts
  the push `kTeSyncOffsetUs` after TE rises (`runner/te_sync.h`). Only
  Unknown Pleasures asks, because it costs up to a refresh of latency a frame.
- The offset (7.4 ms) is the middle of the clean window, found by a sweep:
  eight offsets across one refresh, 3 s each, the step number stamped on the
  screen, filmed at 120 fps. 3.2 to 9.5 ms had no vanished line in 39 updates;
  1.1 and 15.8 ms did, with the seam at film row 495 and film row 268: about 107
  film rows per millisecond (the camera frame is taller than the panel; the
  466-row panel scans about 28 rows per millisecond), so the bad window is only
  about 5 ms wide. It is valid for a full-frame push (the 20.6 ms copy). A push
  of another size moves the flush and the sweep would have to be repeated: the
  QR overlay's 328-row push is one, so a seam may show while the code is up.
  `-DTE_DIAG` logs the TE period and where pushes start.
- `te_sync.c` trusts few edges. Once it knows the period it accepts a rising
  edge only within period/16 of a whole number of periods since the last, so a
  missed edge or a stray pulse cannot move the lock; four misfits in a row drop
  the lock and relearn it. An edge further ahead than one period is stale (the
  32-bit microsecond counter can pass half its range with the line dead), and
  waiting stops 100 ms after the last edge. The ISR is placed in IRAM, but
  Arduino's pin dispatcher and `gpio_get_level` are in flash; that is safe only
  because `CONFIG_ARDUINO_ISR_IRAM` is unset. The run log's `sync=` is the wait
  for the edge and is left out of `push=`: compare `push=` across hacks, and add
  `sync=` to get the frame's latency.
- Reading a film of the display: iPhone slo-mo files store their first and
  last seconds at normal speed, so the label changes every ~100 frames there
  and every 360 in the 120 fps middle. Stabilise against the scenery (four
  corner patches; a mask edge around the display pins phase correlation at
  zero), level the rows, and count a vanish only when a line is missing across
  at least three 24 px windows on one row and not in a settled frame of the
  same update. A detector that finds nothing must also find the event you know
  is there: mine reported zero until a known vanish was used as a control, and
  reported many false events on steep line stretches until settled frames were.
- Every push also dims the screen, by an amount that grows with how far the
  picture scrolled since the last push (issue #68). Unknown Pleasures at
  upstream's speed: the dimmest of 12 bands falls to 0.86 of its settled value
  for about 25 ms (three camera frames at 120 fps) at each push, with or without
  TE sync. Rod sees it as pulsing. The dip by `*speed`, net of a noise floor
  taken inside the quiet part of each cycle:

  | Speed | Dip (points) | Rod |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 0.2 | 1.0 | invisible, "really slow" |
  | 0.3 | 2.3 | invisible |
  | 0.4 | 4.0 | visible |
  | 0.5 | 5.6 | visible |
  | 1.0 | 14.5 | visible |

  - Shipped: `*speed: 0.3` in the registry override, about 0.75 px of scroll per
    push (derived from the hack's timing formula and the push rate, not
    measured). A faster push cannot reach the same step: 1.2 px at full speed
    needs about 10 Hz, and a push is 32 ms beside a 143 to 168 ms step. Rows,
    points and rate matter only through the step: 40 by 50 and 30 by 100 dip
    13 to 14% like the default. The 20-row sparse build (5.7% at about 1.56 px)
    sits about four points under the trend and is unexplained.
  - What it is not, each filmed: the write itself, bus or CPU load (a
    near-static scene pushes the same 466 rows at 5 Hz and does not dip), the
    push path (a copy of the canvas before each push still dips), a global
    dimming (stationary reference patches in the same frame stay steady while
    the strokes dip), and the picture's average level (on the host it changes
    under 1% from one pushed frame to the next in the default build, and more
    in the sparse one, which dips less). CABC was switched off with
    `0x55 = 0` and the dip stayed, but the panel's acceptance could not be
    checked (a review reads the datasheet as calling `0x55` Auto Current Limit;
    M5GFX's `readCommand` is a stub).
  - What it looks like: after a change a pixel takes frames to settle, and a
    rise is slower than a fall. Toggle patches, median over 14 events, 1.00 is
    settled, at the crossing and +1 to +3 frames: black to mid grey 0.69, 0.74,
    0.92, 0.98; mid grey to black 1.00 straight away; dark to mid grey 0.79,
    0.92, 0.93, 0.96. These are camera values, not calibrated luminance. The
    cause is not established: it is a transition-dependent loss, consistent
    with a local display response.
  - Overdrive did not help: newly lit pixels at 120% then the nominal frame gave
    a shallower dip with bright pulses before and after (peak to peak 9 to
    10%, against 8.8%) at a lower push rate. RGB565 clips the boost (an
    effective 1.146, and 7.9% of lit pixels have no headroom), so this is not
    a verdict on overdrive in general.
  - Measuring it: a noise-floor window must sit inside the quiet part of a
    cycle (a reference that runs into the next push's dip inflates the null),
    and a fold over integer periods shorter than its bins leaves empty bins.
    A shift probe must be counted on the host: 1 px sideways along near-
    horizontal lines relit only 20% of the lit pixels, 2 px vertically 94%.
    `dump_main.c` writes ordinary RGB565, so do not swap bytes again when
    reading its dumps. Do not let a reference patch reach the camera's ceiling
    (white read 252 to 255); mid grey read 212. Phone slo-mo files declare
    30 fps: the push period against the serial log's fps gave 120.
  - The probe builds (CABC off, a canvas copy with a vertical shift, reference
    and toggle patches, overdrive, row, point and speed overrides) were
    throwaway build flags on a branch that was not pushed; the comments on
    issue #68 describe each one.
- A hack's returned delay is waited after the push, and only the push counts
  against it, so its own step adds to the frame time: to hold a rate, return
  the target minus the step (`ad_flyingtoasters.c`: 19.5 fps became 28.9).
- PSRAM cost model (`diag/psram_bench.h`, `-DPSRAM_BENCH`): the data cache is
  32 KB, 8-way, 32-byte lines over 80 MHz octal PSRAM, and every miss costs
  about 0.92 us whatever the write size (sequential about 35 MB/s). Firmware
  switches to 64-byte lines (4-way) when a hack starts (`dcache.h`, through
  ROM calls the SDK header says an application should not make): sequential
  passes get about 28% faster and the full-frame push drops from 29 to
  24.8 ms, but a lone short write costs 1.3 us a miss. Pinned A/B, two
  rounds each: Deluxe, Interference, Kumppa, Abstractile +9%, HexTrail +17%,
  Marbling +7%, WhirlWindWarp +6%, Qix and Hexadrop +4%, Gears +3%; Lisa,
  Substrate, XRaySwarm, Pyro, RotZoomer flat. A `sync_to_refresh` hack
  keeps 32 bytes (Unknown Pleasures' offset was swept against the old copy
  time) and so does a hack with `dcache_line32` set in its `HackEntry`
  (Discrete: -5% fps, step 67.9 to 72.8 ms, many short spans). The other core
  is parked in IRAM with interrupts off while the cache is reconfigured
  (`dcache_with_other_core_parked`, over `esp_ipc_call`), as the SDK does for
  flash writes: `noInterrupts()` stops only the calling core.
  `-DDCACHE_LINE32` turns it off for every hack. Compare builds only
  pinned: a free-running lap changes random parameters per visit and showed
  false regressions of 3x on five hacks. A ROM prefetch setting (trigger 1,
  size 0) changed nothing; other settings are untried.
- A hack with `repaints_all` (`hack_entry.h`) draws its next frame while core 0
  pushes the last (`runner/push_overlap.[ch]`, issue #54): two canvases swap
  each frame, the worker pushes the finished one, and the loop credits that
  push's measured duration against the hack's delay. Pinned A/B on the board,
  plain to overlapped: Deluxe 14.0 to 19.0 fps, Compass 18.8 to 29.1, FuzzyFlakes
  18.4 to 28.9, Moire2 16.5 to 26.4, Scooter 22.1 to 28.4; eighteen hacks are
  flagged, five of them GL (grep `repaints_all`, and
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_REPAINTS_ALL`). The step slows by about 5 ms (both cores
  share the PSRAM cache), so the frame is roughly the step, not the longer of
  the two. Rules:
  - Flag a hack only if it never reads the canvas it starts from. The noise
    test and the real-swap test in `test_push_overlap` run every flagged hack
    for 300 frames; 40 frames missed Halo, which the 300-frame run caught. GL
    hacks pass since #118 (see `gl.md`); GraphStat's swap run still fails.
  - Only a gain of 5% or more on a pinned A/B earns the flag. Deco and CCurve
    are paced by their own delays and gained 0 and 2.6%.
  - A hack whose `HackEntry` comes from `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` in the
    byte-identical copy (Truchet, +25%) needs a wrapper to be flagged.
  - Any overlay (name, badge, QR, fps, battery) makes the push synchronous
    while it shows, so the fps overlay reads the plain rate. Read `fps=` in
    the serial log for the overlapped one.
  - Three bugs the spike hit: a redraw from the wait loop must not dispatch a
    second push (it blocked 25 ms), the overlay text canvas wraps one buffer
    and must follow `canvas.px`, and the newest-frame pointer must be dropped
    when a hack starts or Forest's first frame swapped the old picture back.
  - `-DPUSH_NO_OVERLAP` turns it off for every hack (the A side of `ab_flash`).
    The spare canvas is 434 KB of PSRAM; if it will not allocate the firmware
    pushes synchronously.

  RGB565 constants. The canvas holds pixels already byte-swapped into the
  display's order (`rgb565()` returns them that way), and the display runs
  with `setSwapBytes(false)`. A swap done by M5GFX on each push cost 10 ms of
  every frame (#23: pushes of 41-45 ms became 31 ms). `px_swap()` turns a
  canvas pixel into ordinary RGB565 and back: only code that reads colour bits
  needs it (the logo loader, `dump_main.c`, tests). A hue-sweeping palette
  stays a rainbow with its bytes swapped (red, green and blue rotate), so only
  pure black and white, or a colour you know (Maze's red flame, its green
  solving path), expose a wrong order on the device. Host frames cannot,
  since the swap happens in the push; compare them with `px_swap` applied.

  blend, in `point2rgb`) breaks on swapped pixels without a compile error and
  without a crash. `substrate_single.c` swaps at `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground` so the hack sees ordinary RGB565; its golden-frame test
  fails if either is missing. Searching for `XGetPixel` finds none of this:
  dump every hack before and after a pixel-format change and `cmp` the frames.
  Pyro differs by a few hundred pixels, because it sorts projectiles by pixel
  value and so draws overlaps in another order.

  through `canvas_clear`, `canvas_point`, `hspan` or `canvas_paste_rect`

  bypass: it is written straight into `px`, marked by hand, and restored with
  `canvas_paste_rect`, which marks it again so the next push erases it.

  one bounding box around everything written in a `startWrite` batch, so rows
  far apart must not share a batch (two corner pixels cost 11.7 ms together,

import sys, statistics as st
rows=[]; cols=None

    if p[1]=="gap": cols=p[1:]; continue

gaps=[r["gap"] for r in rows]

    print(name, "median/max per phase:")
    for c in ("gap","poll","step","render","tick","sig","newlist","listbody","swap","present","sync","wait","cos"):

    print()
EOF

import statistics as st
def load(n):
    cols=None; rows=[]
    for line in open("$SP/cap_%s.txt"%n):

        p=line.strip().split(",")
        if p[1]=="gap": cols=p[1:]; continue
        if p[1]=="end": continue
        rows.append(dict(zip(cols,map(int,p[1:]))))
    return [r for r in rows if r["gap"]>0 and r["gap"]<500000]
for n in ("40x50_s1","40x100_s1","30x100_s1","40x100_s03"):

    ex=[r for r in rows if r["gap"]>med+8000]
    byflag={}
    for r in ex: byflag[r["flag"]]=byflag.get(r["flag"],0)+1
    tk=[r for r in rows if r["tick"]>0]
    over=[r for r in tk if r["gap"]>med+8000]
    print(f"{n}: median={med/1000:.1f}ms frames={len(rows)} excess(>+8ms)={len(ex)} by flag={byflag}; ticks={len(tk)} ticks with excess gap={len(over)}; excess sizes ms={sorted(round((r['gap']-med)/1000) for r in ex)[:40]}")
    # tick cost vs sync slack
    print("   tick us (p50/p90/max)=",st.median(r['tick'] for r in tk), sorted(r['tick'] for r in tk)[int(.9*len(tk))], max(r['tick'] for r in tk), " non-tick sync p50=",st.median(r['sync'] for r in rows if r['tick']==0))
EOF

content.text:
I couldn't reproduce the 190 ms stall on current `main`, so I haven't changed any code. Four configurations on the board show no tick-linked stall in the loop timeline.

The tree is restored and clean on `fix/134-up-tick-stall`. The diagnostic is saved as `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-rod-build-stopwatch-screensaver/3d31fd73-418f-43d0-8ef0-8369b046207f/scratchpad/stall_diag_134.patch`.

## What I measured

I recorded every loop iteration on the board: gap, poll, step, render, tick, signal, list, swap, present, TE sync and wait. I also counted `cos` calls to recover `nspikes`. I ignored the first frame after boot, which has a roughly 600 ms step that inflates the next gap.

| Config | Median frame | Ticks | Tick cost (median / max) | Ticks with a longer frame | Longest steady-state gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 40x50, speed 1.0 | 168.4 ms | 149 | 12 / 17.7 ms | 1 | +63 ms (once) |
| 40x100, speed 1.0 | 202.1 ms | 99 | 27 / 35 ms | 2 | +34 ms |
| 30x100, speed 1.0 | 168.5 ms | 120 | 23 / 35 ms | 2 | +34 ms |
| 40x100, speed 0.3 (shipped) | 202.1 ms | 59 | 24 / 35 ms | 1 | +33 ms |

- **No 190 ms stall appears in any config.** The film's 40x50 stall isn't reproduced.
- **Frames are locked to the TE refresh.** The 40x50 frame period is exactly 10 refreshes, and the others are whole numbers of refreshes too.
- **Tick cost:** the tick costs 12 to 35 ms, almost all of it `generate_signal`. That is roughly 16 µs per soft-double `cos`, about 700 to 2,100 calls per tick depending on `nspikes` and resolution. List regeneration is about 1 ms, and `glNewList` about 0.15 ms.
- **The tick is absorbed by TE slack.** The TE sync wait shrinks by about the tick's cost on tick frames. Only 1 or 2 of the 59 to 149 ticks per run stretch a frame, by one or two refreshes.
- **Other excess gaps aren't tick-related.** Nearly all of them are a single +17 ms refresh, and they mostly land on non-tick frames. That looks like TE sync landing on a refresh boundary.
- **Why this disagrees with the film (hypothesis, not tested).** The film clips came from the #68 probe builds, which had canvas copies and other changes, not from `main`. A stall of that size could also be in the panel path after `pushImage` returns. My loop timeline only sees time spent in the push, not time on the panel.

## What this means

- The first guess in the issue, soft-double `cos` in the tick, is real cost but isn't a visible stall on `main`. The other two ideas, a single-precision wrapper and spreading the tick over frames, aren't justified by this data. A wrapper would save at most a few ms per tick, inside slack that's already there.
- I'd suggest not "fixing" anything yet. A change here would be unmotivated, and the project's rules say to stop when the data contradicts the premise.

## Decisions for you

1. **Can you see it now?** The board currently holds the diagnostic build at the shipped config (40x100, speed 0.3). If you still see a pause every few updates, or can film it again, tell me. A film of current `main` would settle whether the stall is panel-side.
2. **Re-flash?** The board is on the diagnostic build, not plain `main`. Shall I re-flash plain `main`, or leave it for you to look at first?
3. **Issue comment?** Shall I draft a comment for #134 with the table above, not reproducing on `main`, and the open panel-side hypothesis? I'd post nothing until you've read it.

Shall I also write the memory, journal and social post for the session? I'll do that once you've decided on the three points above.

**What I agree with in the report**
- **Wording.** "Transition-dependent brightness loss, consistent with local display response", not "proved 25 ms LTPS hysteresis". The reviewer's 13.5% sum is a plausibility estimate, not validation. A and B are defined by start and end level, not by a brightness threshold.
- **No flash for 110% overdrive.** Its sharpest point is on the reviewer's "restore on the next regular push" design: the next regular push is about 200 ms away, so it would hold the boost eight times too long. I proposed that without checking the timing.
- **The >100 ms tail.** The 1.4% difference between settled images can be a scene-content baseline, so I won't repeat that claim.
- **Sparse build.** It changes density, geometry and cadence together, so it doesn't prove 7 Hz gives its own factor-of-two.

**The next experiment it proposes**
Three conditions at full scroll speed, with the same renderer, brightness and write shape:

| Condition | Geometry | Cadence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 40 rows × 100 points (baseline, already measured about 14%) | natural, about 4.9 Hz |
| B | 40 rows × 50 points | natural, faster |
| C | same as B | capped to A's cadence with a `*delay` override |

B against C separates "faster pushes" from "different geometry". The hack uses elapsed time, so a longer delay raises the movement per push back to A's, and the clock logic isn't touched. It first needs a host preview of rows and step cost, as the report asks.

def run(path, interval_s):

    dumps=[[]]

    for d in dumps:

content.text:
You were right to point me at that session, and I need to correct my earlier conclusion. The stall is real, but it's a stall in the scroll, not in the pushes.

**What I got wrong.** The previous session's build B was a plain build with only `*resolution: 50`, the same config I ran. Its probe flags were all off. So I measured the wrong thing. My loop timeline shows pushes landing on time every 168.4 ms, but the film detects "pushes" from changes in the displayed image. If a push carries an almost identical image, it looks like a stall.

**The mechanism.** The cause is in `draw_unk` (`unknownpleasures.c:619-625` and `707-711`):
- `ratio = clamp((now - tick) / interval, 0, 1)` sets the scroll position.
- The tick fires at the end of the first frame where `tick + interval <= now`.
- That frame was already drawn with the ratio clamped to 1.0, so the surplus time is lost.
- The tick then sets `bp->tick = now`, so the lost time is never recovered.

The size of the loss depends on how the frame period divides the tick interval. At 40x50 and full speed the interval is 1.2 s and the frame period is 168.4 ms, which gives 7.13 frames. The tick lands 0.147 s late, 87% of a frame, so that frame barely moves.

**Reconstructing the scroll position from my captured timestamps, per config:**

| Config | Interval | Normal step | Step on tick frame (median) | Ticks under half a step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 40x50, speed 1.0 | 1.2 s | 0.140 rows | 0.018 (13%) | 141 of 148 |
| 40x100, speed 1.0 | 1.2 s | 0.168 rows | 0.131 (78%) | 1 of 99 |
| 30x100, speed 1.0 | 1.6 s | 0.105 rows | 0.032 (30%) | 117 of 120 |
| 40x100, speed 0.3 (shipped) | 4.0 s | 0.051 rows | 0.032 (63%) | 2 of 58 |

- **The 40x50 clip fits.** A near-zero step on every tick looks like one push repeated, so the film sees a gap of about 2.1 frames (355 ms against 168 ms), every 7th or 8th push. That matches IMG_5875.
- **The 40x100 default fits.** The tick almost lines up with the frame period, so the pause is small, matching the film's +4 to +6 camera frames.
- **Why it varies.** The stall depends on whether the frame period divides the interval. This also explains why it appeared random and why the 50-point build stalled more than the 100-point one.
- **One piece of evidence doesn't fit.** IMG_5877 (speed 0.4) showed one doubled gap in 28 pushes. My arithmetic predicts only a mild loss there. I haven't explained that one.
- **Not verified directly.** This is arithmetic from measured timestamps and the hack's own formula, not a pixel comparison. A loss of 0.018 rows is about a quarter of a pixel, so the frames would differ slightly. The film's "change stays near 0.5 with no spike" is consistent with that.
- **The `tick_unk` cost isn't the cause.** It takes 12 to 35 ms, absorbed by TE slack as I measured.

**Impact on the shipped build.** At the shipped 40x100 and 0.3 the tick frame moves 0.45 px against 0.7 px normally. That is invisible, so this is a correctness wart on the shipped build, not a visible bug.

**Possible fix.** A wrapper in `unknownpleasures_gl.c`, with the copied hack untouched:
- Rename upstream's `draw_unk` and add a replacement.
- It runs `tick_unk` before rendering when the interval has elapsed, and advances `bp->tick` by exactly one interval.
- The ratio is then continuous across the tick with no clamp loss.

Steps:
- I'd write a host test with a fake clock first. It would show the near-zero step on a tick frame, fail on that, then pass after the change.
- It would change UP's pinned frame hash.
- Open question: whether `glXMakeCurrent` must come before the tick, which I'd check in the shim.

**Decisions for you**
1. Do you want the fix (wrapper plus fake-clock test), or park it given the shipped impact is negligible? I'd lean to doing it, as it's small and general.
2. Shall I re-flash plain `main`? The board still holds my diagnostic build, and I won't flash without your say-so.
3. Shall I draft a #134 comment with the corrected mechanism and the table above? I'd hold it until you've read it.

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

**"Other tests" means the project's suite, not just your file.** A
green run of the test you wrote is not a green suite. Before you call
the change done, run the project's test command (bare `pytest`,
`npm test`, `cargo test` — whatever the repo uses) even when your task
named only one test file. A scope statement in your task bounds the
deliverable, not your verification. Any failure that run shows —
including one you didn't cause — goes in your report by name; a red
test you watched scroll past and didn't mention is a report falsified
by omission.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

When writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:
- Name the production change that would make the test fail — before writing it
- Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior
- Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes
- Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests written after pass immediately — which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)" | Tests-after answer "what does this do?"; tests-first answer "what should this do?" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote — you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |
| "Already manually tested" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. "Worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy — that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. "Pragmatic" shortcuts mean debugging in production — slower, not faster. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

# GitHub Flavored Markdown Generation

**Version:** 1.2.1

Generate GFM that passes markdownlint validation with zero violations.

## Core Principles

### 1. Blank Lines Are Mandatory

- Before/after ALL lists (MD032)
- Before/after ALL headings except document start (MD022)
- Before/after ALL code blocks (MD031)
- Between ALL block-level elements

### 2. Consistency Required

- Use `-` for lists
- Use `#` for headings (ATX)
- Regular spaces only—never tabs/nbsp

### 3. Structure Matters

- Heading hierarchy: 1→2→3 (not 1→3)
- ONE H1 per document
- Files end with one newline
- Lines under 80 chars

### 4. Invisible Characters Matter

- Use ONLY regular spaces (U+0020)
- Never non-breaking spaces (U+00A0,  )
- Never tabs
- UTF-8 encoding

## Pre-Generation Checklist

- [ ] Where will lists/headings/code appear?
- [ ] Heading levels verified (1→2→3)?
- [ ] Using `-` for all lists?
- [ ] Code languages specified?
- [ ] Lines under 80 chars?
- [ ] Line breaks needed? (two trailing spaces)
- [ ] Using regular spaces only?
- [ ] URLs wrapped in `<>` or `[]`?
- [ ] Document starts with H1?
- [ ] Ordered lists use `1.` for all items?
- [ ] File ends with single newline?
- [ ] Tables use consistent spacing?

## Essential Rules

### Lists (MD032, MD004)

```markdown
Text before.

- Item one
- Item two

Text after.
```

### Headings (MD001, MD022)

```markdown
Text.

## Heading

Content.
```

### Code Blocks (MD031, MD040)

````markdown
Text.

```python
code()
```

Text.
````

**Nested Fences:** When showing markdown examples that contain code blocks,
use **one more backtick** than the deepest level:

- Three backticks (` ``` `): Regular code
- Four backticks (` ```` `): Markdown examples with code
- Five backticks (` ````` `): Nested markdown examples

`````markdown
````markdown
# Example

```bash
command
```

````
`````

### Line Length (MD013)

Break long lines at natural points. Use reference-style links for long URLs.

### URLs and Email (MD034)

Wrap bare URLs and emails:

```markdown
Wrong: https://example.com
Right: <https://example.com>
Right: [link](https://example.com)

Wrong: user@example.com
Right: <user@example.com>
```

### Document Structure (MD041)

Start with H1 (or front matter then H1):

```markdown
# Document Title

First paragraph.
```

### Ordered Lists (MD029)

Use `1.` for all items:

```markdown
1. First
1. Second
1. Third
```

### File Endings (MD047)

End with single newline:

```text
Last content line.
[single newline]
[EOF]
```

### Table Column Style (MD060)

Use consistent spacing in tables. Three styles:

**Compact (recommended):** `| cell |` - single space around content

```markdown
| Header 1 | Header 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Data | More data |
```

**Aligned:** Pipes vertically aligned with padding

**Tight:** `|cell|` - no spaces

Pick ONE style per document. Compact is preferred.

### Character Encoding

**Detection:** View → Render Whitespace in VS Code

**Fix:** Find `\u00A0` → Replace with space

**Critical for AI:** Two trailing spaces = intentional line breaks. Do NOT
remove them.

## Critical Error Patterns

### 1. List Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD032 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text:
- Item
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD032 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text:

- Item

Text.
```

### 2. Heading Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD022 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text.
## Head
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD022 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text.

## Head

Text.
```

### 3. Code Without Blanks/Language

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD031 MD040 -->

**Wrong:**

````markdown
Text:
```
code
```
Text.
````

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD031 MD040 -->

**Right:**

````markdown
Text:

```python
code
```

Text.
````

### 4. Inconsistent Markers

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD004 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
- Item
* Item
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD004 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
- Item
- Item
```

### 5. Skipping Levels

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD001 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
# Title

### Sub (skipped H2)
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD001 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
# Title

## Section

### Sub
```

## Post-Generation Validation

1. Lists have blank lines before/after
2. Headings have blank lines before/after
3. Code has blank lines before/after
4. Heading progression: 1→2→3→4
5. All lists use `-`
6. All code has language
7. Lines under 80 chars
8. Document starts with H1
9. URLs wrapped properly
10. Ordered lists use `1.`
11. File ends with one newline
12. Two trailing spaces used intentionally
13. Only regular spaces (no nbsp/tabs)
14. Tables use consistent column spacing

## Mental Model

Markdown is **blocks with mandatory spacing:**

```text
[Text Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Heading Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
```

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

**"Other tests" means the project's suite, not just your file.** A
green run of the test you wrote is not a green suite. Before you call
the change done, run the project's test command (bare `pytest`,
`npm test`, `cargo test` — whatever the repo uses) even when your task
named only one test file. A scope statement in your task bounds the
deliverable, not your verification. Any failure that run shows —
including one you didn't cause — goes in your report by name; a red
test you watched scroll past and didn't mention is a report falsified
by omission.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

When writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:
- Name the production change that would make the test fail — before writing it
- Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior
- Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes
- Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests written after pass immediately — which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)" | Tests-after answer "what does this do?"; tests-first answer "what should this do?" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote — you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |
| "Already manually tested" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. "Worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy — that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. "Pragmatic" shortcuts mean debugging in production — slower, not faster. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

# GitHub Flavored Markdown Generation

**Version:** 1.2.1

Generate GFM that passes markdownlint validation with zero violations.

## Core Principles

### 1. Blank Lines Are Mandatory

- Before/after ALL lists (MD032)
- Before/after ALL headings except document start (MD022)
- Before/after ALL code blocks (MD031)
- Between ALL block-level elements

### 2. Consistency Required

- Use `-` for lists
- Use `#` for headings (ATX)
- Regular spaces only—never tabs/nbsp

### 3. Structure Matters

- Heading hierarchy: 1→2→3 (not 1→3)
- ONE H1 per document
- Files end with one newline
- Lines under 80 chars

### 4. Invisible Characters Matter

- Use ONLY regular spaces (U+0020)
- Never non-breaking spaces (U+00A0,  )
- Never tabs
- UTF-8 encoding

## Pre-Generation Checklist

- [ ] Where will lists/headings/code appear?
- [ ] Heading levels verified (1→2→3)?
- [ ] Using `-` for all lists?
- [ ] Code languages specified?
- [ ] Lines under 80 chars?
- [ ] Line breaks needed? (two trailing spaces)
- [ ] Using regular spaces only?
- [ ] URLs wrapped in `<>` or `[]`?
- [ ] Document starts with H1?
- [ ] Ordered lists use `1.` for all items?
- [ ] File ends with single newline?
- [ ] Tables use consistent spacing?

## Essential Rules

### Lists (MD032, MD004)

```markdown
Text before.

- Item one
- Item two

Text after.
```

### Headings (MD001, MD022)

```markdown
Text.

## Heading

Content.
```

### Code Blocks (MD031, MD040)

````markdown
Text.

```python
code()
```

Text.
````

**Nested Fences:** When showing markdown examples that contain code blocks,
use **one more backtick** than the deepest level:

- Three backticks (` ``` `): Regular code
- Four backticks (` ```` `): Markdown examples with code
- Five backticks (` ````` `): Nested markdown examples

`````markdown
````markdown
# Example

```bash
command
```

````
`````

### Line Length (MD013)

Break long lines at natural points. Use reference-style links for long URLs.

### URLs and Email (MD034)

Wrap bare URLs and emails:

```markdown
Wrong: https://example.com
Right: <https://example.com>
Right: [link](https://example.com)

Wrong: user@example.com
Right: <user@example.com>
```

### Document Structure (MD041)

Start with H1 (or front matter then H1):

```markdown
# Document Title

First paragraph.
```

### Ordered Lists (MD029)

Use `1.` for all items:

```markdown
1. First
1. Second
1. Third
```

### File Endings (MD047)

End with single newline:

```text
Last content line.
[single newline]
[EOF]
```

### Table Column Style (MD060)

Use consistent spacing in tables. Three styles:

**Compact (recommended):** `| cell |` - single space around content

```markdown
| Header 1 | Header 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Data | More data |
```

**Aligned:** Pipes vertically aligned with padding

**Tight:** `|cell|` - no spaces

Pick ONE style per document. Compact is preferred.

### Character Encoding

**Detection:** View → Render Whitespace in VS Code

**Fix:** Find `\u00A0` → Replace with space

**Critical for AI:** Two trailing spaces = intentional line breaks. Do NOT
remove them.

## Critical Error Patterns

### 1. List Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD032 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text:
- Item
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD032 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text:

- Item

Text.
```

### 2. Heading Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD022 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text.
## Head
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD022 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text.

## Head

Text.
```

### 3. Code Without Blanks/Language

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD031 MD040 -->

**Wrong:**

````markdown
Text:
```
code
```
Text.
````

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD031 MD040 -->

**Right:**

````markdown
Text:

```python
code
```

Text.
````

### 4. Inconsistent Markers

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD004 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
- Item
* Item
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD004 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
- Item
- Item
```

### 5. Skipping Levels

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD001 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
# Title

### Sub (skipped H2)
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD001 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
# Title

## Section

### Sub
```

## Post-Generation Validation

1. Lists have blank lines before/after
2. Headings have blank lines before/after
3. Code has blank lines before/after
4. Heading progression: 1→2→3→4
5. All lists use `-`
6. All code has language
7. Lines under 80 chars
8. Document starts with H1
9. URLs wrapped properly
10. Ordered lists use `1.`
11. File ends with one newline
12. Two trailing spaces used intentionally
13. Only regular spaces (no nbsp/tabs)
14. Tables use consistent column spacing

Markdown is **blocks with mandatory spacing:**

```text
[Text Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Heading Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[List Block]
```

/* Builds the unmodified blaster.c with a free that is safe before the first
 * draw. The hack sets NUM_ROBOTS in init but allocates `robots` on its first
 * draw, and its free loops NUM_ROBOTS times over `robots`, so freeing it first
 * dereferences NULL. Two quick button presses can do that. */
#include "screenhack.h"

/* blaster.c registers itself at its end; this file registers it instead. */
#undef XSCREENSAVER_MODULE
#define XSCREENSAVER_MODULE(CLASS, PREFIX)

#include "blaster/blaster.c"

static void blaster_free_safe(Display *dpy, Window window, void *closure) {
  struct state *st = (struct state *)closure;
  if (!st->robots) st->NUM_ROBOTS = 0;
  blaster_free(dpy, window, closure);
}

const HackEntry blaster_hack = {"Blaster", blaster_defaults, blaster_init,
                                blaster_draw, blaster_free_safe};
#define XSCREENSAVER_MODULE_2(CLASS,NAME,PREFIX)			\
									\
  static struct xlockmore_function_table				\
	 NAME ## _xlockmore_function_table = {			\
	   CLASS,							\
	   DEFAULTS,							\
	   WRITABLE_COLORS,						\
	   XLOCKMORE_COLOR_SCHEME,					\
	   init_    ## PREFIX,						\
	   draw_    ## PREFIX,						\
	   reshape_ ## PREFIX,						\
	   release_ ## PREFIX,						\
	   free_    ## PREFIX,						\
	   PREFIX   ## _handle_event,					\
	   & PREFIX ## _opts,						\
	   0,								\
  };									\
									\
  struct xscreensaver_function_table					\
	 NAME ## _xscreensaver_function_table = {			\
	   0, 0, 0,							\
	   xlockmore_setup,						\
	   & NAME ## _xlockmore_function_table,				\
	   0, 0, 0, 0, 0,						\
	   XLOCKMORE_FPS, XLOCKMORE_FPS_FREE,				\
	   XLOCKMORE_VISUAL };						\
									\
  XSCREENSAVER_LINK (NAME ## _xscreensaver_function_table)

#define XSCREENSAVER_MODULE(CLASS,PREFIX)				\
      XSCREENSAVER_MODULE_2(CLASS,PREFIX,PREFIX)

Posted by Claude Code on Rod's behalf, at his request. Update from a
device investigation of this issue.

## The stall is in the scroll, not in the pushes

The cause is not the cost of `tick_unk`, and the pushes are not late. The
picture stops moving for one push at each new row.

`draw_unk` scrolls by `ratio = clamp((now - tick) / interval, 0, 1)`. It adds
a row at the end of a draw, once a frame finds `tick + interval <= now`, and
then sets `bp->tick = now`. The frame that finds the interval over has already
been drawn at the clamp (ratio 1.0), and the clock restarts at that frame's
time, so the time past the interval never scrolls. How much is lost depends on
how the frame period divides the interval: at 40 rows by 50 points and full
speed the interval is 1.2 s and a frame is 168.4 ms, which is 7.13 frames, so
the row is added 87% of a frame late and that frame barely moves. A push of an
almost identical picture looks like a stall on film: 355 ms between changes
against 168 ms.

## What I measured on the board

A temporary build (never committed) recorded every loop: gap, poll, step,
render, tick, signal, list, swap, present, TE wait and wait. At least 30
steady-state ticks per configuration, with the first frame after boot left
out. The scroll step is rebuilt from the recorded frame times and the hack's
own formula.

| Config | Interval | Ticks | Normal step | Step on the tick frame | Ticks under half a step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 40 x 50, speed 1.0 | 1.2 s | 148 | 0.140 rows | 0.018 (13%) | 141 |
| 40 x 100, speed 1.0 | 1.2 s | 99 | 0.168 rows | 0.131 (78%) | 1 |
| 30 x 100, speed 1.0 | 1.6 s | 120 | 0.105 rows | 0.032 (30%) | 117 |
| 40 x 100, speed 0.3 (shipped) | 4.0 s | 58 | 0.051 rows | 0.032 (63%) | 2 |

- The 40 x 50 build loses nearly all of a step at every tick, which is the
  doubled gap every seventh push in IMG_5875. The default 40 x 100 build at
  full speed nearly lines up (1.2 s is 5.94 frames of 202 ms), so its pause
  was small, as filmed.
- On the shipped build the tick frame moves 0.45 px against 0.7 px, which is
  not visible.
- Not explained: IMG_5877 (speed 0.4) showed one doubled gap in 28 pushes,
  and the arithmetic predicts only a mild loss there.
- This is arithmetic on measured timestamps, not a pixel comparison.

## What it is not

- **Late pushes.** The loop period was steady: 168.4 ms (10 refreshes) at
  40 x 50, and a whole number of refreshes in every other configuration.
  Excess gaps were nearly all one refresh (17 ms) and mostly on frames
  without a tick.
- **The cost of a tick.** `tick_unk` took 12 ms (50 points) to 35 ms (100
  points), almost all of it `generate_signal`: about 16 us for each software
  `double` `cos`, 700 to 2,100 of them a tick. The list rebuild was about
  1 ms and `glNewList` about 0.15 ms. The TE sync wait shrinks by about that
  much on a tick frame, so it did not stretch frames. A single-precision
  wrapper is not justified by this.
- **Serial output.** The only logging is the 5 s stats line.

## Fix

A change to `unknownpleasures_gl.c` (the copied hack stays byte-identical)
adds the row before the draw and moves `bp->tick` on by exactly one
interval, so the surplus scrolls the next frame. A host test with a fake
clock fails without it (a frame changed less than half as much as usual) and
passes with it; mutating the fix back to `bp->tick = now` fails the test
again. It is not yet on the board.

- **Test:** the new test in `firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c` drives the hack with a fake clock at the shipped config (`*speed: 0.3`, 40 rows) and a frame period that puts the tick 87% of a frame late. It asserts no frame changes the picture by less than half the typical amount.
- **Docs:** I updated the #134 gotcha in `.claude/rules/gl.md`.

**Verification, reported separately**
- **Red:** before the fix, only the new test failed ("a frame changed less than half as much as usual").
- **Mutation:** I changed the fix back to restarting the clock at the frame's time. That failed both the new test and UP's pinned hash. I restored the file afterwards and checked it matched the original.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Posted by Claude Code on Rod's behalf, at his request. Update from a
device investigation of this issue.

## The stall is in the scroll, not in the pushes

The cause is not the cost of `tick_unk`, and the pushes are not late. The
picture stops moving for one push at each new row.

`draw_unk` scrolls by `ratio = clamp((now - tick) / interval, 0, 1)`. It adds
a row at the end of a draw, once a frame finds `tick + interval <= now`, and
then sets `bp->tick = now`. The frame that finds the interval over has already
been drawn at the clamp (ratio 1.0), and the clock restarts at that frame's
time, so the time past the interval never scrolls. How much is lost depends on
how the frame period divides the interval: at 40 rows by 50 points and full
speed the interval is 1.2 s and a frame is 168.4 ms, which is 7.13 frames, so
the row is added 87% of a frame late and that frame barely moves. A push of an
almost identical picture looks like a stall on film: 355 ms between changes
against 168 ms.

## What I measured on the board

A temporary build (never committed) recorded every loop: gap, poll, step,
render, tick, signal, list, swap, present, TE wait and wait. At least 30
steady-state ticks per configuration, with the first frame after boot left
out. The scroll step is rebuilt from the recorded frame times and the hack's
own formula.

| Config | Interval | Ticks | Normal step | Step on the tick frame | Ticks under half a step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 40 x 50, speed 1.0 | 1.2 s | 148 | 0.140 rows | 0.018 (13%) | 141 |
| 40 x 100, speed 1.0 | 1.2 s | 99 | 0.168 rows | 0.131 (78%) | 1 |
| 30 x 100, speed 1.0 | 1.6 s | 120 | 0.105 rows | 0.032 (30%) | 117 |
| 40 x 100, speed 0.3 (shipped) | 4.0 s | 58 | 0.051 rows | 0.032 (63%) | 2 |

- The 40 x 50 build loses nearly all of a step at every tick, which is the
  doubled gap every seventh push in IMG_5875. The default 40 x 100 build at
  full speed nearly lines up (1.2 s is 5.94 frames of 202 ms), so its pause
  was small, as filmed.
- On the shipped build the tick frame moves 0.45 px against 0.7 px, which is
  not visible.
- Not explained: IMG_5877 (speed 0.4) showed one doubled gap in 28 pushes,
  and the arithmetic predicts only a mild loss there.
- This is arithmetic on measured timestamps, not a pixel comparison.

## What it is not

- **Late pushes.** The loop period was steady: 168.4 ms (10 refreshes) at
  40 x 50, and a whole number of refreshes in every other configuration.
  Excess gaps were nearly all one refresh (17 ms) and mostly on frames
  without a tick.
- **The cost of a tick.** `tick_unk` took 12 ms (50 points) to 35 ms (100
  points), almost all of it `generate_signal`: about 16 us for each software
  `double` `cos`, 700 to 2,100 of them a tick. The list rebuild was about
  1 ms and `glNewList` about 0.15 ms. The TE sync wait shrinks by about that
  much on a tick frame, so it did not stretch frames. A single-precision
  wrapper is not justified by this.
- **Serial output.** The only logging is the 5 s stats line.

## Fix

A change to `unknownpleasures_gl.c` (the copied hack stays byte-identical)
adds the row before the draw and moves `bp->tick` on by exactly one
interval, so the surplus scrolls the next frame. A host test with a fake
clock fails without it (a frame changed less than half as much as usual) and
passes with it; mutating the fix back to `bp->tick = now` fails the test
again. It is not yet on the board.

The fix is flashed and the serial logs look right. In my reconstruction, a new row no longer freezes the scroll. I haven't seen the screen, so that part needs your eyes.

## What was flashed and captured
- The fix, pinned to UP with rotation off, in two configs: 40x50 at full speed (240 s) and the shipped 40x100 at 0.3 (300 s).
- Both flashes verified.
- The board still holds the second one, with the temporary loop recorder in it.
- The working tree is clean at `a19f5f5` and the recorder is saved as a patch in the scratchpad.

## What the logs show
This reconstructs the scroll step from the recorded frame times, as before:

| Config | Ticks | Step on tick frame, before | After | Smallest after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 40x50, speed 1.0 | 163 | 13% | 100% | 90% |
| 40x100, speed 0.3 (shipped) | 60 | 63% | 100% | 100% |

- **No tick frame is under half a step.** It was 141 of 148 and 2 of 58 before; it is 0 of 163 and 0 of 60 now.
- **The solved clock phase is consistent.** The data fixes the clock's phase to a 2 to 9 ms window over about 160 ticks, so ticks are exactly one interval apart.
- **Nothing else moved.** The frame period is 168.3 ms (was 168.4) and 202.2 ms (was 202.1). Tick cost is still 12 to 35 ms, and the TE sync wait still absorbs it.
- **fps:** steady state is at least 6.0 and 5.0. Only the first window after boot is lower.
- **Memory:** heap is flat at 253,676 bytes from the second window, and PSRAM doesn't move.
- **Log hygiene:** the log contains only boot lines and the 5 s stats lines. There are no warnings and no panics.

My first pass at this reconstruction misread the fix. I seeded the clock's phase arbitrarily, which showed tick frames at 248% and 513% of a normal step. I solved the phase from the data, which gave the results above. The solved window being feasible is a real check on the method, but it's still arithmetic and not a film.

## What I'd like you to look at
The board is on UP at the shipped config. At full speed 40x50 the old stall was a doubled gap every seventh push. If you want to see it gone on the panel, that build would need re-flashing. I'd do that on your say-so.

## Drafts
- **Comment:** the draft #134 comment now has an "On the board with the fix" section. It's at `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-rod-build-stopwatch-screensaver/3d31fd73-418f-43d0-8ef0-8369b046207f/scratchpad/issue134_comment.md`. It lints clean apart from the deliberate MD041. I haven't posted it.
- **PR:** I haven't pushed or created a PR. Following `deliver-branch`, it would be: push the branch, create the trail, open the PR as a draft with `Fixes #134`, then read the body back. I'd leave the screenshot placeholder, since the visual check is yours.

## Decisions for you
1. **Post the comment?** I won't post without your approval.
2. **Re-flash?** Shall I put a clean fix build (no recorder) on the board, and if so pinned at 40x50 full speed to look at, or plain rotating `main` plus fix?
3. **Push and open the draft PR?** Say go and I'll do it per `deliver-branch`.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
## Session summary (issue #134, Unknown Pleasures "stall")

### Standing rules and constraints (from the user's CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and statements; they must keep applying)
- The user is Rod Begbie (British spellings, colleague tone). I address them as "Rod", don't flatter, and say plainly when something is unverified or failed. Their pronouns are unstated, so use they/them if needed.
- **Never flash, erase or write the device without Rod's explicit approval.** Ask before every flash or serial open. Keep the `app3M_fat9M_16MB` partition scheme and never touch `ffat`. The serial port is `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401`. Leave `/dev/cu.usbmodem14201` alone. Rod has approved the flashes done so far in this session.
- NEVER post, comment or create undrafted PRs in tools without Rod's express approval. Agent-written comments must disclose upfront that they are from an agent running under Rod's command (the issue's existing style is "Posted by Claude Code on Rod's behalf, at his request."). Open PRs as drafts. Leave `<!-- screenshot placeholder -->` for screenshots.
- Never `git add -A` (use named paths). Never `git commit --no-verify`. Commits end with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. PR descriptions end with `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)`. Verify the branch with `git branch --show-current` before committing. Do not commit while a build is compiling from the working tree.
- **Copied hacks stay byte-identical** to `vendor/`. Changes go in wrappers or the shim. Test first, on the host. Mutation-check new tests. Report "compiles", "host tests pass" and "runs on the device" separately. Only Rod can confirm what the screen shows.
- Use `uv run` and `NO_COLOR=1` for `pio` output. Redirect test output to a file and read the summary line. Never gate a commit on `| tail`. Invoke the `/markdown` skill before writing Markdown. `gh issue view` prints nothing here; use `gh api repos/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/N`.
- Session rituals: at wrap-up, post a reflection to social media (creative username, emojis), write journal insights (journal MCP), and update auto-memory files. These are not yet done this session.
- The deliver-branch skill covers the push, trail create, PR body sync and read-back. Rod's memory notes say Rod says "commit and push it", then "merge", and approves each flash, merge and re-pin.

### Task and investigation outcome
Rod asked to work on issue #134 ("Unknown Pleasures stalls about 190 ms every 7th push"). I used systematic-debugging, then TDD.

**Root cause (found, after my first conclusion was wrong).**
- First I measured loop timing on the board with a temporary recorder (`-DSTALL_DIAG`) and found no push stall. Pushes land on a steady 168.4 ms (10 TE refreshes) at 40x50, speed 1.0.
- Rod then pointed me to the previous session (4c516cba-60f9-4ecc-8569-06298f6abd52, via `entire`). Build B there was a plain build with `-DUP_RES=50 -DROTATE_SECONDS=0 -DSTART_HACK=unknownpleasures`, with all probe flags off. That is the same config I ran, so config alone was not the difference.
- The real cause is in `firmware/src/hacks/unknownpleasures/unknownpleasures.c`. `draw_unk` (lines ~619-625, 707-711) scrolls by `ratio = clamp((now - bp->tick)/interval, 0, 1)`. It ticks at the end of the draw when `bp->tick + interval <= now`, then sets `bp->tick = now`. The frame that finds the interval over was already drawn at the clamp (ratio 1.0), and the clock restarts at that frame's time, so the surplus never scrolls. A near-identical picture is pushed, which the film reads as a stall.
- The loss depends on how the frame period divides the interval (interval = `(0.6/speed)*(80/count)`; the hack halves count at displays of 480 px or less, so 80 gives 40 rows).
- Reconstructed scroll step on the tick frame, before the fix: 13% of normal at 40x50 speed 1.0 (141 of 148 ticks under half a step); 78% at 40x100 speed 1.0; 30% at 30x100 speed 1.0; 63% at the shipped 40x100 speed 0.3 (2 of 58 under half).
- `tick_unk` itself costs 12 to 35 ms, almost all of it `generate_signal` (about 16 µs per software-double `cos`, 700 to 2,100 calls). List rebuild is about 1 ms and `glNewList` about 0.15 ms. The TE sync wait absorbs it, so it never stretched a frame. A single-precision wrapper is not justified.
- Unexplained: IMG_5877 (speed 0.4) showed one doubled gap in 28 pushes, and the arithmetic predicts only a mild loss there.
- The reconstruction is arithmetic on measured timestamps and the hack's own formula, not a pixel comparison or a film.

**Fix (committed locally).** Commit `a19f5f5` on branch `fix/134-up-tick-stall` (created from clean `main`). It is not pushed and there is no PR. It changes three files:
- `firmware/src/hacks/unknownpleasures_gl.c`:
  - Defines `USE_GL` and renames `draw_unk` to `draw_unk_upstream`.
  - Renames the hack's own two function tables via `#define unknownpleasures_xlockmore_function_table up_upstream_xlockmore_table` and `unknownpleasures_xscreensaver_function_table up_upstream_xscreensaver_table`, so it can register its own.
  - Includes `unknownpleasures/unknownpleasures.c`.
  - Defines a replacement `draw_unk` that, when `bp->glx_context && !bp->button_down_p && bp->tick + interval <= double_time()`, does `glXMakeCurrent`, calls `tick_unk(mi)`, then `bp->tick += interval`, and then calls `draw_unk_upstream(mi)`.
  - Registers with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE_2("UnknownPleasures", unknownpleasures, unk)`.
  - `xlockmore.h` has no include guard, so the macro save/restore approach failed. A blaster_safe-style approach was not used.
- `firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c`:
  - New test `test_unknownpleasures_scrolls_through_a_new_row_without_standing_still`. It uses `xshim_set_clock` with its own clock (`scroll_now`, `scroll_clock`), frame period `4.0/19.13` at the shipped 0.3 speed, and 46 frames. It computes picture change as the sum of absolute green-channel differences (`picture_change`, using `px_swap`) and asserts the median is above 0 and the minimum is at least half the median.
  - UP's pinned frame hash is re-taken to `0xe2ab6cf9eec7e74dull`, after I looked at a dumped frame 400 (dump index 52; the `grep -n` recipe was off by one).
  - Registered via `RUN_TEST`.
- `.claude/rules/gl.md`: the #134 gotcha is rewritten to describe the real cause and the fix.
- Commit message references #134.

**Verification, reported separately.**
- Red: before the fix only the new test failed ("a frame changed less than half as much as usual"; 126 of 128 cases passed, the one failure was the new test).
- Mutation: changing the fix to `bp->tick = double_time ()` failed both the new test and the UP hash. The file was restored and checked as identical.
- Host: the full `pio test -e native` passed, 847 of 847.
- Compiles: `pio run -e stopwatch` succeeded (flash 52.7%). `tools/check_notices.py` exits 0. Pre-commit hooks passed.
- Device, with the fix and a temporary recorder:
  - The solved clock phase window was 2 to 9 ms wide over about 160 ticks.
  - The tick-frame step is now 100% of normal. The 40x50 speed-1.0 run had 163 ticks and 0 under half a step (smallest 90%). The shipped 40x100 speed-0.3 run had 60 ticks and 0 under half (smallest 100%).
  - The frame period is unchanged: 168.3 ms (was 168.4) and 202.2 ms (was 202.1). Tick cost is unchanged.
  - Steady-state fps is at least 6.0 and 5.0; only window 0 (boot) is lower.
  - Heap is flat at 253,676 bytes from window 2, PSRAM is unchanged, and the log holds only boot and stats lines.
  - My first fixed-mode reconstruction wrongly showed 248% and 513% because the clock seed was arbitrary. It was corrected by solving the phase from the data. I should report this honestly.

### Temporary diagnostic work (never committed)
- Patches saved in the scratchpad (`/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-rod-build-stopwatch-screensaver/3d31fd73-418f-43d0-8ef0-8369b046207f/scratchpad/`): `stall_diag_134.patch` (against old main) and `stall_diag_134_on_fix.patch`.

- Captures: `cap_*.txt`.
- The previous session transcript was exported to `transcript_full.txt` and `raw_claude.jsonl`. The shared checkpoint is 01M58J0JB2870RZWWK3ZFZR9GN. A Codex session (01a150b3-ae57-7311-a76a-910946739683) on `fix/68-slower-scroll` also exists.

It opens with the agent disclosure, then covers: the stall is in the scroll, the four-config table, what it is not (late pushes, tick cost, serial), the fix, and an "On the board with the fix" section with the before/after table. It lints clean apart from the deliberate MD041. It states that this is arithmetic on measured times, not a film, and that I haven't seen the screen.

I made a temporary edit to `firmware/src/hacks/registry.c` (`*speed: 1.0` and `*resolution: 50` in the UP overrides), built with `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="-DROTATE_SECONDS=0 -DSTART_HACK=\"unknownpleasures\""` and uploaded. The board now holds the clean fix build, pinned to Unknown Pleasures, no rotation, full scroll speed, 40 rows of 50 points, which is the filmed stall config.

### Open threads and next steps
1. Rod validates the fix visually on the board. They would need to say what they see (the doubled gap every seventh push should be gone). Optionally they could film it; I would not open the serial port without asking.
2. Rod's earlier message said that once the flash and serial review were done, "we can update the comment and PR body". The comment draft is updated. Posting needs Rod's explicit approval. If Rod validates, update it to say the screen was checked.
